prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Who, Small, Turn

outputs.L1:
Who could have dreamed them up? At least snails have shells,
but all these possess is—nothing.
Small black antennae, like fat pins, wave
as if they might take in enough to see them through.
Turn them over: they are the soles of new shoes,
pale and unmarked as babies. They flow—
the soil itself learning how to move, and, moving,
almost staying still—their silver monorail
the only evidence of where they have been.
And they die quietly, or at least (mercifully)
beyond the human ear's range, between two stones,
beneath heels, shriveling in salt or piss, at the tips
of sharp sticks. Fight back, I hear myself say,
do something. Don't merely endure it. But they die
as they had lived, exuding slime, like
the smaller boys, who would just
stand there, wretched in short pants,
school socks slumped to their ankles,
school tie unknotted and askew, and flowing
from their noses slow cauls of snot that,
from time to time, they'd lick or sniff back up
part way, until it flowed again, coating
the upper lip, falling into the mouth, mingling
with tears before anything had even been done—
the fear itself enough, so that even had we wished,
we could not have let them off. Sometimes it was
the knee "where you daren't show your mother,"
other times the kick in the shins, the stick across
the head, the punch in the mouth, while they
just stood there, or doubled up, gasping
for breath—and we did it again.
outputs.L2:
Who might have invented such creatures? Snails at least come equipped with shells, yet these possess absolutely nothing. Tiny dark feelers, resembling swollen pins, sway about as though hoping to absorb whatever's needed to survive. Flip them upside down and you'll find the undersides of fresh footwear, pale and blemish-free like infants. They glide along, as if the earth itself were discovering movement, and while moving they nearly remain motionless, that gleaming single track behind them serving as the sole proof of their passage.

Their deaths are silent, or thankfully at least beyond what human ears can detect—crushed between a pair of rocks, beneath shoe heels, dissolving in salt or urine, or impaled on pointed sticks. Defend yourselves, I catch myself telling them, act, don't simply endure it. Yet they perish the same way they existed, oozing their slime, much like those smaller boys who would merely stand frozen in place, wretched in their shorts, their school socks slumped around their ankles, their ties loosened and crooked, while thick veils of mucus streamed from their noses—which they'd occasionally lick or partly snort back inside, before it ran down again, glazing their upper lips, dripping into their mouths, blending with tears before any harm had even come to them. The terror alone was sufficient, so that even had we wished to spare them, we couldn't. Sometimes we struck the knee "where you wouldn't dare reveal it to your mother," other times a kick to the shins, a stick across the skull, a fist to the mouth, while they just stood there, or folded over, struggling to breathe—and we'd strike them once more.
outputs.L3:
# The Parallel Between Snails and Bullied Boys

The poem draws a poignant comparison between the vulnerability of snails and that of small, defenseless boys who suffer at the hands of bullies at school. Through this parallel, the poem explores themes of fragility, helplessness, and the cruelty that is often inflicted upon those least able to protect themselves.

At the heart of the poem lies the depiction of snails as almost shell-less, fragile creatures. So delicate is their existence that the only evidence they leave behind is a faint, silvery trail—a shimmering reminder of a life that passes largely unnoticed. This imagery emphasizes their profound vulnerability and the tenuous nature of their presence in the world.

The snails meet their ends quietly and without ceremony. They are crushed beneath careless heels, dissolved in salt, or destroyed by the jabbing of sharp sticks. These deaths are unremarkable and go unwitnessed, underscoring how easily such fragile lives can be extinguished without consequence or acknowledgment.

The speaker responds to this vulnerability with a sense of frustration, feeling an urgent desire for the snails to "fight back" against their destruction. Yet this impulse only highlights the deeper tragedy: the snails, like the bullied boys, are incapable of defending themselves. This helplessness directly mirrors the plight of the boys who simply endured their abuse, unable or unwilling to resist those who tormented them.

The bullied boys are portrayed with painful vividness—weeping and dripping with snot, they remained passive in the face of their suffering. Cruelly, their visible fear did not earn them mercy but instead provoked their tormentors further, inviting even more aggression. In this way, the poem reveals a disturbing truth about the dynamics of cruelty: vulnerability itself can become a catalyst for further harm, whether the victim is a fragile snail or a frightened child.
outputs.L4:
# The Vulnerability of the Defenseless

This poem draws its power from vivid, unsettling imagery that examines the fundamental defenselessness of snails—creatures that move through the world without any real protection. Though we might imagine their shells offer some safety, the poem presents them as essentially exposed, leaving behind only faint silvery trails as evidence of their passage. These fragile beings die quietly and without resistance, crushed under the careless press of a heel, dissolved by a sprinkle of salt, or prodded to death by an idle stick. There is no drama in their dying, no capacity to fight back—only silent, passive submission to whatever cruelty the world visits upon them.

## The Central Comparison

The heart of the poem lies in the parallel it draws between these helpless snails and vulnerable, weeping schoolboys. Just as the snail cannot defend itself, certain children move through the harsh social world of childhood without armor, their tears and fear marking them as targets. The comparison is deliberately disturbing, for it forces us to confront an uncomfortable truth about how weakness is perceived and treated. The soft, defenseless creature and the crying child occupy the same precarious position: both are at the mercy of those stronger and crueler than themselves.

## The Cruelty of Childhood

What makes the poem so unsettling is the speaker's honest recollection of participating in this cruelty. Rather than positioning himself as an observer or a defender of the weak, the speaker admits to tormenting these passive victims. This confession exposes the disturbing reality of childhood bullying—not as an aberration, but as something the speaker himself engaged in and now examines with troubled clarity.

Most disturbing of all is the poem's central paradox: that the very helplessness and fear of the victims seemed to *invite* further violence rather than compassion. The weeping, the passivity, the visible terror—these qualities, which should provoke mercy, instead seemed to provoke aggression. The tears that might soften a decent heart instead marked the child as prey, just as the snail's slow, defenseless crawl seems almost to beg for the descending heel.

## An Unsettling Truth

Ultimately, the poem reveals something profoundly unsettling about human nature: our aggression toward the weak. By linking the casual destruction of snails to the torment of vulnerable children, the speaker suggests that cruelty toward the defenseless is not merely learned but somehow instinctive—a dark impulse that emerges precisely when we encounter creatures or people who cannot resist us. The poem offers no comfortable resolution, no redemption for the speaker's past actions. Instead, it leaves us sitting with the difficult recognition that vulnerability, far from guaranteeing protection, can dangerously invite the very violence it should prevent.
outputs.L5:
# The Power of Small Turns

Have you ever stopped to consider **who** shapes the direction of your life? Often, we imagine that dramatic, sweeping changes are what define us. Yet more frequently, it is the **small** decisions that quietly steer us toward who we become.

Think about a ship crossing the ocean. A **turn** of just a single degree may seem insignificant at first. But over hundreds of miles, that tiny adjustment can mean the difference between arriving at your destination or drifting far off course. Our lives work in much the same way.

**Who** we are tomorrow is built from the **small** choices we make today. The decision to read a page instead of scrolling endlessly, to speak a kind word instead of a harsh one, or to take a short walk instead of staying seated—these are the modest **turns** that add up over time.

It is easy to overlook these moments because they feel too **small** to matter. We wait for the perfect opportunity, the big break, or the grand transformation. But real growth rarely announces itself. Instead, it hides in the quiet **turns** of daily habit.

So the next time you wonder **who** you want to become, remember that greatness is not found in one massive leap. It lives in a thousand **small** turns, each one gently guiding you toward a better version of yourself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that begins by describing slugs and their vulnerability, then unexpectedly shifts to a memory of childhood bullying, drawing a connection between the creatures and the weakest boys at school.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt**

They have no shell, no place to hide,
these soft and glistening things
that leave their silver signatures
across the morning's damp.

You could crush one with a careless step
and never know the weight
of what you'd ended—all that slow
determination, gone.

A boy once brought a shaker
to the playground in his fist.
We watched him find them in the grass
and season them like meat.

They curled. They foamed. They shrank into
themselves and disappeared,
and we all laughed, or some of us,
the ones who weren't afraid.

But there was always one boy smaller,
softer than the rest,
who moved the way the slugs did—slow,
too easy to be found.

I think his name was Thomas. Or
I've made that name to fill
the hole where I forget him now,
the way you can forget.

We had our salt as well. Our words,
our shoving in the line.
And I was neither cruel nor kind—
I only watched, and lived.

The slugs come back each spring, you know.
They always find the wet.
But Thomas, or whatever name—
I never saw him after.

I wonder if he grew a shell.
I hope he grew a shell.
I hope he doesn't leave a trail
that anyone can follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem exploring cruelty and complicity, using the image of slugs dying in various ways as a metaphor for how children bully the meek.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Salt Taught Us

We were small then, and cruelty came easy
as breathing—easier, maybe.

Behind the toolshed we made a science
of small deaths. The slugs came out after rain,
soft as tongues, trailing their silver
apologies across the concrete.

Marcus brought the salt.
Someone always brings the salt.

We watched them fold into themselves,
those slow bodies dissolving
into froth, and we laughed
the way you laugh when something
gives you permission.

There was a boy named Daniel
who moved like that—soft,
too soft, leaving himself visible
in every hallway.
We were the salt for him.

I never brought it.
I want that on record.
I only stood there,
hands in my pockets,
watching the shrinking,
saying nothing,
which is its own kind of pouring.

Some slugs we drowned.
Some we let the ants find,
carrying them off in pieces
while we grew bored and wandered
toward the swings, already
forgetting.

That's the part they don't tell you—
how forgetting is the final cruelty,
how the meek get twice erased:
once in the doing,
once in how easily
we walk away.

I think of Daniel now
and cannot remember his face,
only the salt,
only my clean and useless hands,
only how silence
has no residue,
leaves no silver trail
to follow back
to where I stood
and let it happen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, unsettling poem that moves from natural observation to a confession about participating in schoolyard violence against smaller, weaker boys.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Field Teaches**

The hawk works the low field in autumn light,
patient as arithmetic. It knows
the small things live by staying still,
so it waits for the tremble in the grass,
the vole that cannot help its own soft heart.

I watched this from the fence line as a boy
and understood it without words:
the world sorts itself by weight.
The frost took the tender plants first.
The wind chose whatever couldn't hold.

I want to say I learned this only from the field.

There was a boy named Peter, small enough
that his coat swallowed him, whose voice
went up when he was frightened, which was often.
We found the higher pitch of it hilarious.
We were a weather, then. We were the frost.

I never threw the first punch. I want that
counted somewhere—I only stood
and made the ring of bodies that becomes a cage,
and laughed the laugh that keeps a laughter going,
and did not lend him the one thing he needed,
which was a single face that wasn't grinning.

I told myself I was the grass, not the hawk.
But the grass does not applaud the killing.
The grass does not go home and sleep,
and I slept. God help me, I slept fine.

Now every autumn when the hawk comes down
I feel the old thrill leap up in me first—
that clean, uncomplicated wanting—
and only after, like a slower animal,
the shame that has his small face still,
still asking the ring of us
to open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem in the style of a British poet reflecting on slugs, snot-nosed schoolboys in short pants, and the guilt of childhood bullying.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Salting**

We found them after rain, the slugs,
their slow processions on the wall,
grey pilgrims trailing silver rugs
of slime toward some sodden hall.

And we were nine, in itching grey,
short trousers chafing scabbed pink knees,
snot glazed and crackling like the day
was made for cruelties like these.

Someone brought salt. I won't pretend
I stood aloof, a saintly lad—
I watched them foam and writhe and end,
and something in me half was glad.

But there was one boy, softer, small,
who wept for slugs and would not throw.
We salted him against the wall
of laughter. Forty years ago.

I don't recall the slugs at all,
their froth, their shrivelling, their pain—
but him I keep: his snuffling, tall
in memory as a weathervane

that swings above me, points, accuses.
The rain comes on. I'm grey myself.
The mind selects; the heart still bruises;
guilt sits, a jam-jar, on the shelf.

And children still, in every yard,
find something smaller than their fear
and press it flat. The lesson's hard:
we salt to prove we're standing here.

I'd say I'm sorry. He is gone,
or grown, or dead, or does not care.
The slugs come out. The rain comes on.
I leave the salt cellar where it is,
and let them cross the evening air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an extended, single-stanza poem that begins with tender curiosity about slugs and slowly turns into a disturbing recollection of collective cruelty toward defenseless victims.
counterfactuals.output:
They come out after rain, the slugs,
and I have always wondered how they choose
their slow direction, what soft compass turns
inside that boneless ribbon of a body,
how they carry the whole wet architecture
of themselves across the cold flagstones,
antennae testing the dark like a blind man's fingers,
leaving behind that silver signature of passage—
and as a child I would crouch to watch them,
marveling at the patience, the sheer defenselessness,
the way they asked for nothing but to cross,
and it is here the memory begins to sour,
for I remember, too, the other children,
the salt shaker passed from hand to hand
like something sacramental, the delight
that rose in our small throats as the creature
folded, foamed, diminished, that terrible science
we performed without a name for what we did,
and how easily the tenderness became a game,
how the same crouch that once was reverence
became the posture of the executioner,
and no one stopped us, no one thought to,
because they were only slugs, we said,
they cannot even scream, we said,
and that, I think, was exactly why we chose them,
because a thing that cannot cry for mercy
teaches us how little mercy we contain,
and I have carried that silver trail of knowledge
across the years, the way they carried themselves
across the stones, slow, deliberate, unforgiven,
still asking nothing but to be allowed to cross.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
